ModelFamily.description: Statistical model family used to estimate the effect. Open vocabulary: write the source's own wording in the field when nothing here fits.
ModelFamily.title: ModelFamily

ModelTerm.description: One term of the model: a column of the design matrix, or the equivalent predictor in a family with no design matrix. A categorical term names its levels and the entities carrying them; a continuous term carries the facts that make a slope interpretable. Nothing here is a fact about any one contrast -- what a contrast did with this term is a `Cell` on that contrast's Effect. A term with no cell on some contrast is a term that contrast was adjusted for rather than tested.

assessment.description:
The assessment whose measurements supply a continuous term, **including when the column is derived from them rather than being one of them**: a change score, a percent change, a composite of subscales, a residualized score. The instrument is still where the values came from, and one administration or several makes no difference to that -- `region` says the same by example, an ROI mean and a PPI regressor both naming their region.
One instrument, one record, however many columns it supplies: two subscale scores of one questionnaire each name it, and which subscale a column carries is the term's `name`.
Unset only when the values come from somewhere the study does not record as an Assessment -- age, dose, a motion parameter, cardiac phase, scanner drift -- in which case `source_definition` names the origin. A term with neither is a column whose origin the record does not state.

functional_form.description:
Shape of the term's relationship to the measure. A squared term with a negative coefficient is an inverted-U relationship, not a negative association, so non-linear and transformed terms must not be recorded as linear. A model fitting both a linear and a quadratic form of the same measurement has two terms, not one.
Not where a product is recorded: a non-empty `interaction_with` is what makes a column a product.

id.description: Stable identifier, referenced by an Effect's `cells` and its `mediation.mediator`, and by `interaction_with`.

interaction_with.description:
The other terms this term is a product of -- what makes this column an interaction column. Populate it when the source names an interaction term in one model; leave it empty when the source describes a regression on a contrast.
The terms it may name are those of this model and of the stages it reaches through `inputs_from`, which is how a group stage crosses a cohort factor with a first-level condition: the product column is declared where it was fitted and names the lower stage's column directly.
A crossing of two factors is normally read off the cells, since a factor compared against itself carries a positive cell and a negative one. A continuous term has no levels and so cannot be crossed that way, which makes this slot the only record of a moderation such as `age x group`; the derived kind reads it before `variation_level`.
A product of terms that are all categorical and all crossed is legal but decides nothing, the crossed cells already saying what it says, and is flagged for review.
A product column declares no `levels` of its own; a signed cell on one with a continuous component may name a level of the factor, saying whose slope the sign describes. Such a column is not a covariate of a contrast whose cells name all of its components.

levels.description: The levels of a categorical term, and for each the entities carrying it. This is the whole of what a factor is: its level vocabulary, and which cohort, condition, occasion, or arm occupies each cell. Record a level the source names even when no reported contrast uses it -- a three-level factor contrasted at two levels is still a three-level factor. Empty for a continuous term.

name.description:
Term label, unique within the model: a name appearing twice is one term recorded twice. For a categorical term this is the factor's identity.
Often a label the source never writes. A paper reporting 1-back, 2-back and 3-back conditions states the levels and states that they vary together, but frequently names no axis; `load` is then a name supplied for a grouping the source does make. That is permitted, within two limits: the levels must be source-stated, and the name must not assert a comparison or a construct the paper does not.

region.description:
The region whose signal supplies this term: a seed timecourse, an ROI mean covariate, a PPI physiological regressor. The counterpart of `assessment` for a column drawn from a place in the brain rather than an instrument.
Singular, so it does not serve a factor that *compares* regions: that is one term with several levels, and the regions hang off `FactorLevel.regions`.

source_definition.description:
The source's own definition of the term, and the origin of a continuous term that no Assessment supplies, such as age, dose, a motion parameter, cardiac phase, or scanner drift.
**Required for a derived column, whatever its `assessment` says.** A change score names its instrument in `assessment` and its derivation here, in the source's own words and including the occasions it spans -- "percent reduction in BDI, (post-pre)/pre, from baseline to post-treatment". Nothing else can carry those occasions: `FactorLevel.timepoints` names the occasions a factor *compares*, and a derived column has no levels to hang them on, so where a study has several post-intervention occasions this is the only thing separating a change to the endpoint from a change to a later follow-up.
Not the shape of the fitted relationship, which is `functional_form`: a percent change entered linearly is a linear term computed from a difference, so recording the construction as the form would lose whether the fit was linear or quadratic. A transform *of the measure* the vocabulary cannot name still goes in functional_form.

type.description:
Whether the term is categorical or continuous. Categorical when the column distinguishes named cells of the design -- occasions, cohorts, conditions, arms, regions -- whether or not the paper names the axis; `levels` is then required. Continuous when the column carries a measured value and the model fits a slope.
Small as it is, this field settles four others: whether `levels` exists, whether a `Cell` here takes a `level`, whether the term can be crossed, and which branch of the derived kind fires. A term recorded continuous is one no contrast can be built across.
**A term whose name states a comparison -- `pre > post`, `A versus B` -- is almost always a categorical factor written down from its contrast's side.** The design matrix distinguished two occasions, cohorts or conditions; the paper labelled the difference and left the axis unnamed. Record the factor with a level per side and let the cells carry the direction (`representing-models.md` §5.6). Collapsed into one continuous column, nothing says what was compared and the effect reads as a slope.
The exception is a column genuinely holding one number per participant -- a difference score, a percent change entered as a covariate. That is continuous, and `source_definition` records the subtraction it came from.

unit.description: The unit a continuous term is measured in, when the source gives one -- years for age, mg for a dose. It is what makes a reported slope interpretable.

variation_level.description:
Whether this term moves within a participant or only across the sample. Populate it for **any** term: a repeated-measures factor is within-subject and a diagnosis factor is between-subject in exactly the sense a trial-wise modulator and an age covariate are.
For a continuous term it is what separates a parametric modulation from a cross-subject regression, and the derived kind of any effect testing it reads this on that basis. For a categorical factor it feeds no derivation, so setting it changes no other value; it is the factor's scope, and two studies that crossed a factor within participants and between them did not estimate the same thing.
A categorical factor's levels usually settle it, and the two should agree: levels naming `groups` are between-subject, since a participant belongs to one cohort; levels naming `timepoints` are within-subject, since an occasion is when the same people were measured again; levels naming `conditions` are within-subject in the ordinary repeated-measures case; levels naming `arms` follow `StudyDesign.assignment_structure`, crossover being within and parallel between.
A level the vocabulary cannot name is written here as free text; the derived kind then cannot choose between a modulation and a regression, so it is undetermined for that record rather than wrong.

PerformanceMetric.description: One reported performance measure of a decoding analysis, and its value.

name.description: The measure as the source names it, such as accuracy, balanced accuracy, AUC, d-prime, sensitivity, specificity, or a correlation between predicted and observed scores.

reference_value.description: Numeric reference this measure was compared against, when reported -- chance for an accuracy, zero for a correlation. relation.description: Direction of this measure relative to its own reference_value.

description.description: Narrative overview of the pipeline, its inputs, outputs, and intended purpose.

id.description: Stable identifier used by Analysis foreign-key references.

smoothing_fwhm_mm.description: Full width at half maximum of the applied spatial smoothing kernel, in millimetres: a list of one value for an isotropic kernel and of three for an anisotropic [x, y, z] one. Record 0 when the source states that no smoothing was applied.

Region.description: A brain region the study delimited and used: a connectivity seed or target, the search space an analysis was restricted to, a level of a factor comparing regions, or the signal a model term carries. atlas.description: The atlas, parcellation or template it came from, as named -- AAL, WFU_Pickatlas, Schaefer 400 -- with version or parcel index when given. `definition_method: atlas` records that one was used, not which, which is not enough to pool two studies.

definition_method.description: How the region was delimited, which is a statement about independence: one drawn from the study's own prior contrast is not independent of an effect tested inside it. name.description: The region as the source names it -- aSCC, left dlPFC parcel, salience network. Its own words: normalization to an anatomical vocabulary happens downstream and needs the original to map from.

region_type.description: What kind of thing the region is, which `definition_method` does not settle: an atlas parcel and an anatomical structure can both come from an atlas, and a network is neither.

RegionDefinition.description: How a region was delimited, which records independence: a region drawn from the study's own prior contrast is not independent of an effect tested inside it. Open vocabulary: write the source's own wording in the field when nothing here fits.

RegionType.description: What kind of thing a region is. Open vocabulary: write the source's own wording in the field when nothing here fits.

ResponseModality.description: How participants responded during a task. Open vocabulary: write the source's own wording in the field when nothing here fits.

ResultReporting.description: Whether a paper reports inferential analyses of its own.

SampleSource.description: Where a participant group came from. Closed, because the three cases carry different consequences for pooling and a fourth would be a judgement rather than a source.

SecondBlock.description:
What a decomposition crossed the brain block with, one value per block. This decides whether two decompositions answer the same question, so it is the payload's one required vocabulary -- a task PLS and a behavioural PLS are not poolable, and neither is a one-block ICA with either of them.
Multivalued, and `none` is a value rather than an absent field: a one-block decomposition is a positive assertion, not a gap. Name the blocks and not their number -- a design-plus-behaviour PLS is `[design, behavioral]`, and the count follows from the list's length.
Open vocabulary: write the source's own wording in the field when nothing here fits.

SimilarityDetails.description: Payload for a representational-similarity analysis. The direction of a model-brain association is a continuous ModelTerm on the analysis's ModelEstimation, with the model RDM as the term, tested by the Effect through a `Cell`. Before choosing this family, check that the association is at the RDM level: a similarity regressor entered into a univariate GLM is a parametric modulation, not RSA.

competing_models.description: Other models the reported model was compared against.

details_type.description: The concrete details subclass carried by this payload. Populated from the class itself, not extracted.

model.description: The model RDM tested. Unset for a genuinely model-free test, such as within- versus between-category pattern similarity, or dissimilarity against zero -- a single signed cell rather than a comparison.

neural_representation.description: How the neural pattern was defined, such as the voxel set or time window used.

similarity_metric.description: Similarity or distance metric. The RDM distance metric and the model-brain association method are different facts, and crossnobis values are not comparable with correlation-distance values.

SimilarityDetails.title: SimilarityDetails

degrees_of_freedom_denominator.description: Denominator degrees of freedom, used alone for t, correlation, and chi_square. Both are unset for z. Float, so corrected degrees of freedom such as a Greenhouse-Geisser adjustment can be recorded as reported.

degrees_of_freedom_numerator.description: Numerator degrees of freedom, normally populated only for f and likelihood_ratio. A single-degree-of-freedom statistic leaves this unset, since t(151) is F(1,151).

family.description: The statistic used, independent of the thresholding procedure. A t-test corrected by permutation is still a `t`.

Statistic.title: Statistic

StatisticFamily.title: StatisticFamily

coordinate_space.description: The space this image is in. Recorded per map because a study can share maps in a different space from the one its tables report.

description.description: Notes about map provenance, processing, or relation to the reported result.

id.description: Stable identifier for this map record, assigned by the pipeline.

is_thresholded.description: Whether the available map has already been thresholded.

map_type.description: Content type, such as statistic, effect estimate, variance, z-score, t-score, or thresholded label map.

statistic_type.description: Statistical quantity encoded by the map, when applicable.

url.description: Resolvable location of the map or its archive landing page.

Study.description: The publication-level record that contains the groups, tasks, design, acquisitions, preprocessing pipelines, model estimations, analyses, and reported result tables belonging to one study. Conditions belong to the task they are part of, not to the study.

acquisitions.description: Image or signal acquisition protocols used in the study.

analyses.description: Distinct analyses or inferential tests reported by the study, including those that found nothing (`Analysis.outcome: no_significant_effect`) and those reported without coordinates. Whether an empty list means the paper reports none is `result_reporting`'s to say, not the list's.

assessments.description: Measures of participants that were taken independently of an acquisition.

authors.description: Authors of the study or publication, in published order.

coordinate_sets.description: Every group of coordinates the paper reports, in its tables or its text, with what each is for.

description.description: Brief free-text summary of the study aims and scope.

design.description: The study's design outside its tasks: how participants were assigned, the arms they were assigned to, and the occasions data were collected on. The narrative design description is this record's own `description`.

devices.description: The scanners, amplifiers, or recording systems the study collected data on. Declared here once and referenced by identifier.

doi.description: Digital Object Identifier, without requiring a particular URL form.

external_datasets.description: Named external datasets used, cited, or made available by the study.

hypothesis.description:
The study's own statement of what it expected to find, quoted from the paper -- usually the closing paragraph of the Introduction, in the form "we hypothesized that" or "we predicted that". Verbatim but for citation markers, one entry per prediction, so a study stating several gets several.
A prediction, not a purpose. "The aim of this study was to examine whether connectivity differs between patients and controls" says what was tested and takes no value here; "we expected connectivity to be lower in patients" says what was expected and does. Recording an aim as a hypothesis asserts a direction the study never committed to, which is precisely what a reader consults this field to check.
Absent when the paper states no prediction, which is common: never paraphrase an aim, an abstract sentence, or a finding into one. Where the only statement is in the Discussion -- "consistent with our hypothesis that connectivity would be lower" -- quote that clause, which is still the study's account of what it predicted rather than `Analysis.interpretations`, the source's account of what it found.

id.description: Stable identifier for the study record, such as a DOI-based or repository-local identifier.

inference_settings.description: Thresholding and correction schemes used by one or more analyses. Declared here once and referenced by identifier.

language.description:
Languages of the article, as the E-utilities API reports them -- the three-letter codes PubMed assigns, `eng` and the rest. Filled from the same `esummary` call that fills `study_type`, and not read off the paper: the text a reader is given is in one language whatever the article is indexed as.
At least six of the benchmark's sixteen meta-analyses state "English language" as an inclusion criterion, and it was unexpressible. On the 1,804 records measured it excludes exactly one paper, so it buys precision rather than recall; the criterion is stated, so the field states it.

measures.description: The scientific quantities the study measured, used by one or more analyses. Declared here once and referenced by identifier.

model_estimations.description: Model estimation records used by one or more analyses.

outcome_summary.description: What the study's analyses found, taken together: derived from `result_reporting` and the `Analysis.outcome` of every result analysis, so a study whose every analysis is null can be found and described as such rather than vanishing with its missing coordinates.

preprocessings.description: Preprocessing pipelines applied before statistical analysis.

publication_year.description: Year in which the study was first published or made publicly available.

regions.description: Brain regions the study delimited and then used -- as connectivity seeds or targets, as the search space an analysis was restricted to, as the levels of a factor comparing regions, or as the signal a model term carries. Declared here once and referenced by identifier wherever used.

result_reporting.description:
Whether the paper reports inferential analyses of its own. An empty `analyses` list is otherwise ambiguous: a methods or data paper that tests nothing and a paper the extractor read badly look the same. With this set, `no_analyses_reported` asserts the emptiness, with the sentences that show it as evidence.
Says nothing about whether the analyses found anything; that is each `Analysis.outcome`, summarised in `outcome_summary`.

study_type.description: PubMed publication types for this record, verbatim as the E-utilities API returns them (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/help/#publication-types). Multivalued because PubMed assigns several: every article is `Journal Article` and the design of the study motivates other labels.

tables.description: Publication tables from which results or analysis metadata were extracted.

tasks.description: Task, resting-state, stimulation, passive-viewing, or other meaningful participant paradigms associated with study acquisitions. Each holds the conditions it was made of.

title.description: Full title of the study or publication.

Study.title: Study

StudyDesign.description: The design of the study; how participants were assigned, what they were assigned to, and the occasions on which data were collected. The arms and timepoints it holds are referenced by identifier from Condition and Group.

allocation.description:
How participants came to be in the arm they were in.
Its own vocabulary, and not its neighbour's. A study with no arms takes `not_applicable` here -- "nothing was administered, so allocation does not apply" -- and says `observational_cohorts` in `assignment_structure`. Writing `observational_cohorts` into this slot was measured on 4 of 5 freshly extracted observational papers: the value is accepted, because the vocabulary is open, and it answers a different question than the one asked. This slot is the only record of whether anything was administered at all.

arms.description: The arms of the study, active and comparator alike. Every reference to an Arm elsewhere is by identifier, so this list holds the records themselves.

assignment_structure.description: How the compared cohorts came about. Ask first whether anything was *administered or assigned* at all: where nothing was, the answer is `observational_cohorts` and the study has no arms. Only where something was does the rest of the question apply -- separate cohorts, or the same participants passing through several arms -- and that is what says whether an arm reference belongs on a Group or a Condition.

blinding.description: Who was kept unaware of the assignment.

description.description: Overall study design in narrative form, including observational or interventional status, cross-sectional or longitudinal structure, allocation, and blinding when applicable.

timepoints.description: The occasions on which data were collected.

StudyDesign.title: StudyDesign

StudyType.description: PubMed publication types, spelled as the E-utilities API returns them so that a value needs no translation. Only the design-relevant types are listed; PubMed also returns funding and indexing types, and the vocabulary is open, so any unlisted type passes through verbatim.
StudyType.title: StudyType

Table.description: A publication table that supplies coordinates, statistics, or contextual metadata. Raw cell structure and point-level provenance may remain in the repository's coordinate-table representation and be linked with source_path.

caption.description: Table caption describing the table's contents.

column_headings.description: Ordered leaf column headings retained to aid interpretation of extracted values.

coordinate_count.description: Number of reported coordinate rows or points in the normalized table representation.

coordinate_space.description: Coordinate reference space applying to points in **this table**, from the table parser. Per table, because one analysis's tables can be parsed in different spaces, and that disagreement is a fact about the tables worth keeping rather than one to resolve here. `Analysis.coordinate_space` is the space of the analysis and takes priority where the two differ.

description.description: Summary of the table contents and its role in the reported analyses.

footer.description: Table notes, abbreviations, threshold statements, and footnotes.

id.description: Stable table identifier used by Analysis foreign-key references.

purpose.description:
What this table is for. `reported_effect` when its rows are the foci of a tested effect, which is the common case and which is derived from the analyses that name the table; otherwise what the rows are instead -- region or ROI definitions, atlas parcels, connectivity seeds, the peaks of a decomposition's components, coordinates cited from other papers, a stimulus list, demographics, descriptive statistics with no test.
A coordinate table is not an analysis merely by having coordinates in it, and this is the only field that says which it is. Absence means nothing decided: a table deliberately encoded as a non-analysis and one no pass considered are otherwise the same silence, and the coordinates of the first belong on the entity they locate (a Region's description) rather than on a contrast that never produced them.
A per-table answer, so it cannot be right for a table whose row groups serve different purposes -- results beside the ROIs they were tested in. Each row group states its own role in a `CoordinateSet`.

source_path.description: Repository path or external location of the raw or normalized table representation. Set by the ingestion pipeline.

table_number.description: Printed identifier such as Table 2 or Supplementary Table S4.

title.description: Table title, when distinct from the caption.

Table.title: Table

TablePurpose.description: What a table is for. A coordinate table is not an analysis merely by having coordinates in it: a study's ROI definitions, its atlas parcels, its connectivity seeds and the peaks of its independent components are all locations rather than findings, and `reported_effect` is what says the rows ARE a finding. Open vocabulary: write the source's own wording when nothing here fits.
TablePurpose.title: TablePurpose

Task.description: A meaningful participant paradigm, such as a task, resting-state protocol, stimulation, or passive viewing, performed in association with an acquisition. A Task record is required wherever the study models conditions, a resting-state protocol included. Acquisitions with no paradigm do not require one, even in a longitudinal or interventional study: a structural comparison across occasions is carried by the Effect's timepoint terms and linked through Analysis.acquisitions.

acquisitions.description: The acquisition protocols used to collect data for this task. Exclude structural scans unless they are part of the task itself.

conditions.description: The conditions this task was made of. These are the different states/modes of the task.

description.description: Complete narrative description of what participants experienced and did.

design_type.description: How the task's events were modelled in time. Open vocabulary: write the source's own wording in the field when nothing here fits.

instructions.description: Task- or paradigm-specific instructions given to participants.

name.description: Short, unique label for the task or paradigm; corresponds conceptually to BIDS TaskName when applicable.

paradigm.description:
The name with every qualifier that says how this version varies taken off and moved to its own field: `Stroop task` for an emotional Stroop task, `flanker task` for an auditory flanker task, `n-back task` for a food-picture n-back, `incentive delay task` for a monetary incentive delay task. The same as `name` when nothing qualifies it.
This is the extractor's split, made the same way in every paper. Whether the stem or the qualified name is the paradigm is not a fact one paper can state; it is decided across the corpus, in `paradigm_category`.

paradigm_category.description: The paradigm this task is grouped under, decided by task normalization across the corpus rather than read from one paper. The stem in `paradigm` when the corpus shows it varied -- `Stroop task` once an emotional, a counting or an auditory Stroop appears beside it -- and the qualified name when that variant is the only form ever seen. Citations sharpen the call: tasks whose `reference_ids` lead back to the same originating paper belong to one lineage. An outside vocabulary such as the Cognitive Atlas is a noisy suggestion, filtered against the corpus, never the authority on which variants are paradigms.

performance_measures.description: Behavioral variables recorded and summaries used to verify task performance.

presentation_software.description: Stimulus-presentation software name, version, and operating system when reported.

reference_ids.description: `references` resolved to the works they cite, as DOIs or PMIDs, through the parsed paper's reference list. What links a task to the paper that introduced it and to the adaptations that cite that paper, so a task's lineage can be followed.

references.description:
Works the source cites for this task, exactly as it writes them: an author-year citation or a bracketed reference number, kept in the source's own punctuation. Copy the in-text citation; do not resolve, expand or look it up.
Multivalued -- a task may cite the paradigm's origin, an adaptation, and the stimulus set separately. Empty when the source cites nothing for the task.

response_modality.description: How participants responded. Multivalued because a paradigm often collects more than one -- a button press for accuracy and a spoken report afterwards.

stimuli.description: The materials presented to participants, in the source's own terms -- the stimulus set, its name, how many items. One entry per distinct material; `stimulus_modality` carries the sensory channel.

stimulus_content.description: What the task's stimuli were about when that holds across all its conditions -- food pictures at every n-back load, emotional words throughout a Stroop -- which `Condition.stimulus_content` leaves unset because it does not tell the conditions apart. The task-level half of the stimulus facet: a meta-analysis can ask for food stimuli across paradigms, or for Stroop tasks across stimuli, without either question splitting the other.

stimulus_modality.description:
The sensory channel the stimuli were delivered through. Multivalued because a paradigm may use more than one -- a photograph with a spoken label.
Often not stated in those words: a source naming IAPS, NimStim, Ekman faces or film clips has said `visual` without using the word. Inferring it from such a cue is intended, and the cue is what belongs in the evidence -- not the whole methods section.

variant_qualifiers.description: The words of `name` that `paradigm` leaves out, each with the axis it varies the paradigm on. Each is also stated in its own field: a stimulus-content qualifier in `stimulus_content`, a modality qualifier in `stimulus_modality` or `response_modality`, a timing qualifier in `design_type`. Empty when `paradigm` equals `name`.

Task.title: Task

TaskQualifier.description: One word or phrase of a task's name that varies its paradigm rather than naming it: the `emotional` of an emotional Stroop task, the `auditory` of an auditory flanker.

qualifier.description: The qualifier as the name prints it.

TaskQualifier.title: TaskQualifier

TaskVariantAxis.description: What a task-name qualifier varies about its paradigm. Open vocabulary: write the source's own wording when nothing here fits.
TaskVariantAxis.title: TaskVariantAxis

TermType.description: Whether a model term is categorical or continuous.
TermType.title: TermType

Timepoint.description:
One occasion on which data were collected, and where it sits relative to the intervention. Declared once on `StudyDesign.timepoints` and referenced by identifier; `FactorLevel.timepoints` is the only slot that references one, so it is the whole of how an occasion reaches a model.
A study that *compared* occasions did so with a `ModelTerm` whose levels name them, paradigm or no paradigm. An occasion no level references was collected but never modelled: legitimate where the record only describes when follow-up happened, a defect where the analyses report change over time, which `validate_record.py` flags. Names stay in the source's wording; what is normalized is where an occasion sits and in what order.

name.description: Short occasion label as the source states it, for example baseline, post-treatment, six-month follow-up.

order.description: Position of this occasion in the study's sequence, counting from 1. Carries the ordering that `relation_to_intervention` cannot when several occasions share a relation -- the earliest `post_intervention` occasion is the study's endpoint, later ones are follow-ups.

relation_to_intervention.description: Where this occasion sits relative to the intervention. Required, so an occasion the source does not place still carries the slot, as `extraction_status: not_reported`.

time_from_intervention.description: Elapsed time between the intervention and this occasion, in the source's own words and units, for example 24 h or six weeks.

Timepoint.title: Timepoint

TimepointRelation.description: Where an occasion sits relative to the intervention. Directional terms over these values mark an analysis as a within-person change rather than a cross-sectional comparison. Open vocabulary: write the source's own wording in the field when nothing here fits.
TimepointRelation.title: TimepointRelation

VariationLevel.description:
The level at which a term varies -- whether it moves within a participant or only across the sample. A property of **any** term, categorical or continuous: a repeated-measures factor and a trial-wise modulator are both within-subject, and a diagnosis factor and an age covariate are both between-subject.
For a continuous term it is what separates a parametric modulation from a cross-subject regression, and the derived kind of an effect testing it reads this. For a categorical factor it feeds no derivation; it is the factor's scope, and two studies that crossed a factor within participants and between them did not estimate the same thing. Open vocabulary: write the source's own wording in the field when nothing here fits.
VariationLevel.title: VariationLevel
